---

If my own voice falters, tell them hubris was merely my way of adoring you.

The hollow husk of you, once so feverish in life, now cut open,
Reveals ten thousand rags of music within your thoracic cavity.

The hands, received bagged, show upon examination no injury.

Winter, then—the body cold to the touch, unplunderable,
Kept within its drawer of old-world harrowing. Teeth in fair repair.

Will you be buried where; nowhere.
Your mouth a globe of gauze and glossolalia.

And opening, most delft of blue—
Your heart was a mess:
A mob of hoofprints where the skittish colts first learned to stand,
Catching hold of their agility, a shock of freedom, wild-maned.

The eyes bear hazel irides, the conjunctivae pale,
Marked with hemorrhaging. One lung, smaller, congested with rose smoke.
The other, filled with a swarm of massive sentimentia.

I adore you still more. I know
The wingspan of your voice—that whole gorgeous flock of harriers—
Cannot be brought down. You would love this now: this snow, this hour.
Your visitation here tonight, not altogether unexpected.

The night-laborers, immigrants all, gather here, aching for to speaking,
Longing for to work.

---

I preserved the deliberate tonal collision between clinical/autopsy diction and elegiac imagery, as this contrast appears central to the poem's emotional power. I also kept the closing dialectal phrasing ("aching for to speaking," "Longing for to work") intact, as it carries important characterization and voice that would be lost through conventional grammatical correction. Let me know if you'd like a version leaning further toward either the clinical or lyrical register, or adjustments to specific lines.

# On the Autopsy of Devotion: A Reading of the Poem's Central Tensions

The poem opens with an audacious rhetorical gesture: the speaker names their own devotion as a kind of hubris, an excess that borders on transgression. Rather than simply confessing love, the speaker turns outward, challenging the reader or an unnamed interlocutor to account for this adoration should the speaker's own words prove inadequate. This framing does something subtle and important—it positions love not as a private, ineffable feeling but as a phenomenon so extreme that it demands external witness and explanation, as though the intensity of feeling exceeds what any single voice, even the one experiencing it, could articulate alone. The admission of hubris also casts a shadow of guilt or self-awareness over the poem from its very first lines, suggesting that to love this fiercely is itself a kind of overreaching, a defiance of proportion or restraint.

This tension between excess and containment finds its structural counterpart in the poem's central formal strategy: the collision of two radically different registers of language. On one side stands the clinical, forensic vocabulary of the autopsy report—hands bagged, teeth noted to be in fair repair, conjunctivae hemorrhaging. This is language stripped of feeling, designed for precision and detachment, the vocabulary of a body reduced to evidence, to data points on a table. On the other side runs a lyrical, almost incantatory stream of imagery—music, colts, flocks of birds—language that gestures toward the ineffable, the emotional, the alive. The poem does not allow these two registers to remain separate; instead, it forces them into uncomfortable proximity, letting the sterile procedural language of death examination bump up against and interrupt the surge of feeling that the lyrical imagery carries. The effect is jarring by design: it enacts, at the level of form, the very violence the poem describes—the reduction of a once-vital, feeling body into an object of clinical scrutiny.

Nowhere is this collision more vivid than in the poem's treatment of the heart and lungs. Rather than describing these organs in anatomical terms, the poem imagines them as sites of chaotic, overflowing vitality—filled with the hoofprints of skittish colts, swarming with what the poem calls "sentimentia," a term that seems to fuse "sentiment" with the swarming, insect-like connotations of a plague or infestation. This image suggests that the body, even now laid open on the examiner's table, once contained an inner life of such intensity and abundance that it could not be tidily organized or explained—only glimpsed through metaphors of movement, unruliness, and multiplicity. The colts' hoofprints imply restless, undomesticated energy; the swarm of sentimentia implies an emotional excess that could not be counted or contained, only felt as an overwhelming presence. In this way, the poem insists that what the autopsy measures and records is only the residue of something far larger and wilder than clinical language can capture.

And yet, despite the coldness of the examination table and the finality that death imposes, the speaker refuses to let love be conquered by this reduction. The poem asserts, against all the evidence of mortality laid out in forensic detail, that love remains unconquerable—an assertion made through a striking image: the beloved's voice compared to a flock of harriers, birds of prey that "cannot be taken down." This comparison suggests something both fierce and evasive about the beloved's voice—it is not passive or fragile but predatory, resilient, capable of eluding the very forces (death, dissection, clinical language) that would seek to still it. The harrier image thus becomes the poem's central act of resistance: even as the body is opened, catalogued, and rendered into clinical prose, the voice—and by extension the love it inspired—refuses to be grounded, refuses to be brought down to the level of mere evidence.

The poem's final movement widens its scope beyond the individual body being examined, extending its meditation outward to encompass a broader human condition. In its closing image, night-laborers and immigrants gather together, described as aching to speak and longing to work. This shift suggests that the poem's concerns are not confined to a single death or a single love but resonate with a larger, collective experience of unfulfilled voice and unmet longing. Just as the beloved's body once held an excess of feeling that clinical language could not capture, so too do these laborers and immigrants carry within them desires and voices that remain unspoken, unheard, or unrealized. The poem thus closes by drawing a connection between the intimate, particular grief of the autopsy scene and a wider social reality of longing—suggesting that the tension between what is felt and what can be articulated, between vital inner life and the reductive systems that seek to measure or contain it, is not merely a personal tragedy but a condition shared across bodies, borders, and lives.

# Report and Requiem

**CASE NO. 4471-B**
**SUBJECT:** Female, 34 years
**EXAMINATION DATE:** October 14

The body is that of a well-developed, well-nourished female. Rigor mortis is complete. Lividity is fixed and consistent with the position in which the body was found.

*Oh, but you were never still. Even in sleep your fingers moved like they were finding chords on some instrument only you could hear, some music that lived beneath your skin and asked to be let out.*

External examination reveals no signs of trauma to the head or neck. The scalp is intact; hair is dark brown, measuring approximately eleven inches in length.

*Your hair—I used to bury my face in it after long days, breathing in cedar and rain, and you'd laugh, that low rolling laugh like a river finding its way around stones, patient, inevitable, alive.*

The eyes are closed. Corneas are clear. No petechial hemorrhaging is noted in the conjunctivae.

*Your eyes were the color of storm clouds gathering over the bay in November—gray-blue and full of weather, full of something about to break open into light. When you looked at me I understood why sailors trusted the sea even after it had drowned men they loved.*

The chest is opened via standard Y-incision. The ribs are intact. The lungs are pink-gray, unremarkable, weighing 410 grams (right) and 380 grams (left).

*Here—here is where the song lived. Here is where you held your breath before the high note, the one that used to make the birds outside the window go quiet, as if even they knew to listen, as if even the sparrows understood that some voices are a kind of grace that doesn't ask permission to exist.*

The heart is examined in situ. No evidence of infarction. Valves are competent. The heart weighs 290 grams, within normal limits for body habitus.

*Two hundred and ninety grams. That's what they say. But I held that heart in metaphor for six years and it weighed everything—weighed mornings and mercy and the particular way you said my name like it was a note you were still learning to hit perfectly, and each time you got closer, and each time I fell further.*

The stomach contains approximately 200 mL of partially digested food material. Contents are unremarkable.

*You had toast that morning. Just toast, and the coffee you always made too strong, and you complained about it, the way you complained about everything small so you'd have room in your heart for complaining about nothing large at all. That's what devotion sounded like in your house. Small grumbles. Big love.*

The brain is removed and sectioned. Weight: 1,340 grams. No gross abnormalities noted. Gyri and sulci show normal pattern for age.

*Where does a person go? Not the meat of thought, not the wet gray architecture they're weighing on a steel scale, but you—the quick of you, the wit, the way you'd hum Debussy while doing dishes like the sink was a concert hall and the world was lucky to overhear. Where does that go, when it isn't here?*

**PRELIMINARY CAUSE OF DEATH:** Pending toxicology and histological findings. No immediate cause identified on gross examination.

*They will find nothing, because there is nothing to find. You didn't die of organs failing—you died the way birds die in autumn, quietly, mid-flight almost, called somewhere else by a season none of us can follow yet. And still I hear you. In wind through the maples. In the specific hush before rain. In music—God, especially in music, in every minor key that ever made me ache—there you are, unweighable, unsectioned, uncontained by any incision, any scale, any Latin term for absence.*

*They can open the body. They cannot open the love.*

*That stays closed around me like a hand, like a held note, like the sound a bird makes when it finally, finally comes home to roost—not in a body, not in the cold examined flesh of what was—but in the ongoing symphony of every small remembering, every hum of a familiar song, every gray sky that makes me look up and think: there. There you are. Still singing. Still, impossibly, mine.*

---

**FINAL DISPOSITION:** Body released to family for burial services.

*But I have already buried nothing that mattered. That part of you flew off before they even drew the sheet.*
outputs.L5:
# Winter Reveals

There's a peculiar honesty to winter that other seasons lack. When the leaves fall and the landscape strips itself bare, winter reveals what has been hidden all along—the architecture of trees no longer disguised by foliage, the contours of hills once softened by summer green, the bird's nest that seemed invisible in June suddenly exposed in the crook of a branch.

This revealing quality extends beyond the physical world. Winter has a way of exposing truths we might otherwise avoid. The long nights and quiet days leave more room for reflection, whether we seek it or not. Without the distractions of outdoor gatherings and endless daylight, we're left alone with our thoughts more often, and what winter reveals about ourselves isn't always comfortable. It might show us how we've been avoiding something, or how resilient we actually are when circumstances demand it.

There's also something winter reveals about community and connection. In the cold months, people often turn toward each other differently—checking on elderly neighbors, sharing warm meals, finding reasons to gather indoors. The season strips away the casual, breezy interactions of summer and asks for something more intentional. Winter reveals who shows up when conditions are difficult, both in nature and in relationships.

Even the natural world seems to operate under different rules in winter. Animal tracks in snow reveal movements that would otherwise go unnoticed—the fox that crossed the field at dawn, the rabbit that paused near the fence line. The snow becomes a kind of record-keeper, revealing stories that vanish with the next thaw.

Perhaps what winter reveals most profoundly is our relationship with endings and beginnings. The dormancy of the season isn't death but rest, a reminder that revelation doesn't always mean discovery of something new—sometimes it means seeing clearly what was always there, waiting beneath the surface for the right conditions to become visible again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal poem that blends the clinical language of an autopsy report with a tender, grief-stricken love letter to the deceased.
counterfactuals.output:
**REPORT OF POSTMORTEM EXAMINATION**
*Subject: You. Always you.*

**I. EXTERNAL EXAMINATION**

The body is that of a well-developed—no.
Let me start again.

The body is that of someone who once laughed
so hard at 2 a.m. that the neighbors complained,
and I told them *sorry, sorry*, but I wasn't.
I would apologize for anything
except the sound of you being happy.

Height: as tall as the space you left in the doorway.
Weight: immeasurable, since grief
has its own gravity, its own units.

There is a birthmark on the left hip
shaped like a country I have never visited
but now will never stop touring
in the dark, with my eyes closed,
fingers reading you like braille
that spells nothing but *stay.*

**II. INTERNAL EXAMINATION**

Upon opening, the heart is found
to weigh more than the textbooks allow—
this is not unusual. Love adds density.
Grief adds more.

The lungs, when sectioned, release
the smell of your last exhale,
which I have been trying to breathe back in
for months, for years, for the rest
of whatever this is now.

Stomach contents: half a sentence
you never finished. Something about
the future. Something about *us.*
I have been chewing on it since.

**III. TOXICOLOGY**

Blood alcohol: none.
Blood *me*: still present, still circulating,
though the vessel that carried it
has stopped.

I test positive for you
in every room of this house.
I test positive for you
in the coffee cup you left,
the ring it stained into the counter
like a wedding band the wood now wears
because I couldn't.

**IV. CAUSE OF DEATH**

Undetermined.
Or: everything. Or: nothing sudden—
just a slow forgetting how to keep going,
which no one wrote down in time.

I would like to amend the record.
Cause of death: *I wasn't there enough.*
Cause of death: *the world kept spinning
and didn't ask permission.*

**V. MANNER OF DEATH**

They want one word.
Natural. Accidental. Undetermined.

I offer instead: *inevitable, and unbearable,
and still, somehow, love.*

**FINAL NOTES**

The body has been released.
The heart has not.
It remains here, in the drawer
marked *evidence*,
in the freezer of my chest,
in the report I keep amending
at 3 a.m., in longhand,
in the only language
I have left to speak to you:

clinical, precise, and utterly,
utterly ruined.

counterfactuals.output:
**Report on the Beloved, Filed Under Migration**

I.
They open the chest the way a hymnal falls open —
to the page most read, softened at the spine.
*Heart,* the notes say, *enlarged, chambers dilated,*
as if love were only ever a matter of room,
of how much a small red house can hold
before the walls give in to weather.

I say: nightingale. I say: the throat of April.
I say the muscle kept singing long after the wing forgot how to lift.

II.
*Lungs congested, moderate hemorrhage, lower lobes.*
Somewhere a flock goes over, dark as ink flung at a window,
and I think of breath as a flightpath,
each inhalation a bird returning to a country
it no longer recognizes.
Blood pooled like the low note in a cello,
the one that lives underneath the melody,
holding everything up without asking to be heard.

III.
*Cranial vault intact. Subdural hemorrhage, left temporal region.*
Here is where the music entered
and could not find the door back out.
Here is where she heard, once, someone say her name
the way you'd call a sparrow down from a wire —
softly, so it wouldn't startle into sky.

I keep looking for the wound that is only tenderness
turned inward, calcified, mistaken for damage.

IV.
*Contusions, upper extremities, consistent with defense.*
As if the arms were only ever wings
that never got the chance to open fully —
folded too long against a body
built for leaving, kept instead
in the small room of being needed.

V.
*Liver: pale, fatty change. Kidneys: petechial hemorrhaging.*
Small constellations. Little frozen flocks
mid-migration, caught between one country and the next,
the body a night sky no one thought to chart
until it was the only map left.

VI.
I want to tell the examiner: measure this instead —
how she hummed while doing dishes,
how the birds came to the sill each morning
because she'd trained them, patiently, with bread,
to trust an open hand.

But there is no column for adoration.
No box to check for *loved, and how.*
Only the ribs, unlatched like a rusted birdcage,
only the silence where the door swings,
only the space where something
used to lift, and lift, and lift.

VII.
*Cause of death: pending further examination.*

I write instead: she flew.
I write: the last note of the song
is not an ending but a held breath
waiting for the room to answer it.

I write: here lies the instrument.
The music has already gone ahead,
already crossed the water,
already nesting somewhere
we have no clearance to follow.

# REPORT ON THE DISSOLUTION OF THE BELOVED
*(a body, examined)*

---

**I. IDENTIFICATION OF THE DECEDENT**

Thou wast known to me by scars and small
mercies—*decedent presents as*
a white male, thirty-and-some years, *identity confirmed by*
the crook of thy smile which I would know
in any darkness, any drawer, any
cold tray beneath fluorescent
judgment.

Wherefore this clipboard. Wherefore this
Latin where once there was thy name
spoken soft against my throat at 3 a.m.,
*height five foot eleven, weight*
one hundred sixty pounds *of thee reduced*
to figures, to the tare of flesh
without its animating salt.

---

**II. EXTERNAL EXAMINATION**

The hair, dark brown, *normal male pattern*—
I twinned my fingers in it once
beneath an April rain that doth
not fall in reports, only in memory's
unlicensed weather.

*Eyes: irides brown, corneas clear*—
thine eyes that held whole autumns, held
the ochre and the going-under-light
of every dusk we spent unlearning
loneliness. Now: *clear. bilateral.
unremarkable.*

The hands—O the hands I anointed
with what oil love keeps hid—
*exhibit no defensive wounds,
nails short, clean, without polish*—
hands that built me a doorframe once
and could not, in the end, hold the door
against whatever visitor
came calling in the night unnamed.

---

**III. INTERNAL EXAMINATION**

*The heart weighs three hundred forty grams.*

Three hundred forty grams: as if
that were the sum, the total ledger
of what beat in thee each time I entered
a room and thy face did its small
weather-change toward joy.

*Chambers unremarkable. Valves
competent.* Competent!—as though
love were a function graded, passed,
a mere mechanics of the blood
and not the whole cathedral wherein
I once knelt and did not know
I prayed.

*Lungs: pink-tan, crepitant,*
edges sharp—thou breathedst me in
like weather, like the first
cold morning of October, and I
did not think then of *crepitant*,
did not think of *edges*, only
of thy chest beneath my palm
its rise, its fall, its rise—

---

**IV. TOXICOLOGY**

*Blood alcohol: negative.
Opiates: negative. All screens: negative*—

so it was only thee, then. Only
the ordinary catastrophe
of a heart grown tired of its own
weather, no villain, no
substance to blame, no
*it was the poison* to point toward
and say *there, there is the wound
I can name.*

Anon I must accept: sometimes
the body simply doth cease,
the way a clock doth stop not
from malice but from having told,
faithfully, too long, the same
relentless hour.

---

**V. CAUSE OF DEATH**

*Cardiac arrhythmia, etiology
undetermined.*

Undetermined!—as though I
were not standing here, determined,
determining, unmade
by the word *undetermined*—

as though grief were not itself
a cause, a mechanism, an
*acute and chronic* failure
of the world to hold thee longer,

as though love left no residue
detectable, no trace
element the tox screen misses,
being made of nothing
but attention, but the daily
small increments of choosing thee
above all else—

*no findings.*
*no findings.*

---

**VI. MANNER OF DEATH**

*Manner: natural.*

Natural—as though there were
a manner unnatural to losing thee,
as though some deaths were fitting
and this one, too, must be filed
under *ordinary,* under
*the body's clock, its quiet
appointment kept*—

but I say unto this report,
unto its boxes and its blanks:
there is no box for how the morning
after didst arrive the same
insufferable gold, the birds
unmourning in the eaves,
the world continuing its plain
administrative hum
as if a man had not just
ceased to be the axis
around which my whole
weather turned.

*Signed. Sealed. Case closed.*

Not closed. Not closed.
I keep it open like a wound
the coroner cannot suture,
like a drawer that will not
lock, like thy name
which I still say
into rooms
that answer
only
with the silence
of a proper
noun
un-
housed.

**Findings**

*The body is that of a well-developed male/female measuring—*
and here the report forgets you have a name,
forgets the way you said *good morning* like an apology,
forgets your hands, which held oranges like small suns.

Liver: 1,400 grams. Unremarkable.
But I remember you cooking with too much garlic,
laughing when the smoke alarm sang along.

*Lividity fixed, purple in the dependent regions—*
you, dear, always slept on your left side,
curled like a question no one answered.

Heart: enlarged. Signs of old scarring.
Yes. I could have told them that.
I watched you carry it for years
like a suitcase too heavy to check.

*No evidence of foul play.*
Only the foul play of decades,
of rent and fever and the slow arithmetic of hours
that added up to this table,
this light, too bright, too kind for what it reveals.

I keep wanting to write *beloved* in the margins
where the doctor wrote *lungs: congested.*
I keep wanting the Latin to soften into psalm.

*Time of death: approximate.*
As if love ever kept precise hours.
As if I did not feel it exactly
when the room went quiet
and the quiet had your shape.

They will fold you back into yourself now,
sew the incision like a hem,
send you home in a box built for silence.

Outside, dawn is still an hour off.
The city exhales its long grey breath,
and somewhere men and women who speak in borrowed vowels
are mopping floors, stacking crates, wiping down
the counters of a world that barely knows their names—
their hands, too, cataloged only by what they lift,
their hearts unmeasured, their weight unspoken,
carrying the night on their backs
like something holy no one thought to write down.

# Necropsy of a Winter Love

The colt died standing up, the way
brave things unlearn their falling—
legs locked like church doors, mane
still combed by wind that didn't know
to stop. I found him in the lower field,
frost already writing its report
across his open eye: *dilated,
fixed, consistent with*—

consistent with the way you left,
actually. No struggle in the tissue.
Just a slow uncoupling, cell from cell,
the way snow releases from a branch
not because it chooses to
but because the branch
has simply had enough of holding.

Harriers cut grey commas in the sky
above us both—the horse, the girl
who came to touch his cooling flank
and thought of your hands, how they'd once
mapped my body like a coroner
maps cause of death: *thorough,
clinical, unable to explain
the actual moment of the stopping.*

I want to tell you love is not
a pathogen, though it moves
through blood like one—
though it leaves its lesions,
its telltale scarring on the valves,
the kind they find in autopsy
and murmur *chronic,
this had been going on for years.*

The harriers don't mourn.
They simply drop, talons open,
take what the snow reveals—
small deaths made visible
by whiteness, by the way
absence has a color
and that color is this field,
this horse, this letter I won't send
that reads like a report:

*Subject presented with symptoms
of having loved you. Prognosis
was always terminal. Time
of death: ongoing. Contributing
factors: everything. The snow.
The birds. The way winter
undresses a body
to show what it was hiding all along—
that we were dying this whole time,
sweetly, the way frost
kills a field by making it
beautiful first.*
